analysis.one_liner: Caps all consumer credit fees and interest at 36% a year, covering payday, overdraft, and card fees alike.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, where it sat without action and died at the end of the 111th Congress without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written a national maximum into federal law: no lender could charge a consumer more than 36% a year once every fee was counted — interest, late fees, overdraft fees, credit insurance, and add-on products. That would have effectively ended most payday lending, car-title lending, and fee-heavy overdraft programs, and made any loan above the cap unenforceable, with criminal penalties for violators. It also would have required credit card statements to show this all-in rate, labeled 'FAIR,' instead of an APR that hides fees. The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers who rely on payday loans, car-title loans, refund anticipation loans, and overdraft credit — typically lower-income households — would gain a hard ceiling of 36% on the total cost of credit, with loans above that limit void and unenforceable [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Borrowers using payday and overdraft credit

how_it_helps.text: It imposed a national maximum of 36% on the combined fees and interest a creditor can charge a consumer, closing loopholes that let payday and overdraft lenders charge hundreds of percent in annual terms.

Loans made in violation of the cap become unenforceable: the borrower owes nothing beyond principal returned, and violations carry criminal penalties of up to one year in prison or a fine of up to $50,000 per violation.
State attorneys general could enforce the cap in court, and state laws offering stronger protections were explicitly preserved.
Monthly credit card statements would have to show the all-in 'FAIR' rate instead of an APR that excludes many fees.

analysis.who_pays: Payday lenders, banks collecting overdraft fees, tax-refund lenders, and other high-cost creditors would lose the revenue stream the bill's own findings valued at more than $25 billion a year; some marginal borrowers could also lose access to short-term credit entirely [S3].

drawbacks.text: A hard 36% cap covering all fees would likely force many payday, car-title, and overdraft lenders out of business, which could leave some borrowers with no access to short-term credit at all rather than cheaper credit.

The bill offered no alternative small-dollar lending program to replace the high-cost products it banned; it only stated that affordable alternatives 'should be encouraged' [S3], leaving a possible gap in credit availability.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit would have been substantial for low-income borrowers who pay triple-digit effective rates on short-term credit. The costs: some lenders would exit the small-dollar market, and some consumers with poor credit might lose access to any credit at all rather than gain cheaper credit; critics also argued a hard cap does not address why people need such loans in the first place. The bill never advanced far enough for Congress to weigh these tradeoffs.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to its Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 19, 2009 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote ever took place.
It drew 19 cosponsors, all Democrats, out of 253 House Democrats — a small fraction of the chamber.
With the 111th Congress ending on January 3, 2011, any bill not reported out of committee dies; this one was never reported.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Payday, car-title, overdraft-fee, and tax-refund lenders kept charging rates far above 36%, since the bill died before reaching any vote. Consumers who use those products continued paying the fees the bill's findings put at over $25 billion a year.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High-cost lenders kept charging triple-digit rates

for.name: Rep. Jackie Speier
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cap all consumer credit fees and interest at 36% and referred it to committee.

for.name: Rep. William Delahunt
for.what_they_did: Joined the introduction of the bill.

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no report — leaving it to die in committee.

sides.party_line_note: All 19 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican support appears in the record, and the Democratic-controlled Financial Services Committee took no action either.

industries.note: Their business model of charging 300-400% annual rates would be criminalized; loans made above the cap would be void and unenforceable. The bill's findings cite roughly $8.6 billion a year in payday loan fees [S3].
Overdraft charges, which the bill found can run up to 3,500% annualized and total about $17.5 billion a year, would count toward the 36% cap [S3].
The bill found consumers pay nearly $900 million a year in fees on refund anticipation loans, which would be capped [S3].

The headline effect on mainstream credit cards was limited since most card rates were below 36%, but junk-fee-heavy subprime cards would be constrained and statements would have to display the all-in rate [S2].
